strengths: The paper addresses an important efficiency problem: the large visual-token prefix processed by multimodal language models. Reusing visual-encoder attention and keys for adaptive selection and merging provides a simple integration strategy without requiring a separately learned selector.

PruMerge+ offers a useful reported accuracy–compression tradeoff. With 25% of visual tokens, the 7B model achieves 76.8 versus 78.5 on VQAv2, 57.1 versus 58.2 on TextVQA, and 64.9 versus 64.3 on MMBench. These results have practical value even without matching the full model on every benchmark.

Evaluation covers six image benchmarks, two language-model sizes, and three video benchmarks. The training-free Video-LLaVA results are encouraging, particularly the ActivityNet-QA improvement from 45.3 to 48.3 with PruMerge.

The component and training ablations provide meaningful evidence: token supplementation improves MME from 1221.6 to 1350.3, while LoRA adaptation improves the complete method from 1250.1 to 1350.3. The manuscript identifies its principal model and data sources and acknowledges lossy compression and limited validation scale.
weaknesses: The performance-preservation claims exceed the evidence at aggressive compression. In Table 1, 7B PruMerge drops from 78.5 to 72.0 on VQAv2, 85.9 to 76.3 on POPE, and 1510.7 to 1350.3 on MME, despite additional fine-tuning. Similar degradation appears for 13B. These are substantial losses for the affected tasks. PruMerge+ supports a more favorable tradeoff at fourfold token reduction, but does not establish performance preservation at the headline fourteenfold compression.

Practical acceleration remains insufficiently validated. Table 2 explicitly reports roofline estimates for LLM prefill rather than measured execution. There are no measured end-to-end latency, throughput, or peak-memory results incorporating the visual encoder, attention extraction, clustering, and autoregressive decoding. Corresponding efficiency measurements for PruMerge+, which provides the strongest accuracy results, are also missing. The analysis supports potential computational savings but does not establish their realized magnitude.

The comparisons do not adequately establish the contribution over stronger token-reduction alternatives. Table 4 compares against taking the first tokens and uniform spatial sampling. Table 5 supports supplementation but does not isolate adaptive IQR budgeting from ordinary attention ranking. Comparisons against fixed-budget top-k attention selection and an adapted established merging method such as ToMe, under matched token budgets and tuning conditions, would directly test the central methodological claims. The broad statement that previous work has not considered visual-token count also needs qualification given the cited Q-Former and resampler approaches.

Important implementation inconsistencies prevent confident reproduction. Algorithm 1 adds m spatial samples to m outliers, which would approximately double the stated 5.5% retention, yet Table 1 reports 25% for PruMerge+; its subsequent loop and output still enumerate only m tokens. The merging update also excludes the selected center and replaces it with an unnormalized neighbor sum as written, despite the weighted-averaging description. The neighborhood size k, attention-head aggregation, and LoRA hyperparameters are unspecified, and Section 3.3 names final-layer keys while Algorithm 1 specifies the penultimate layer. These ambiguities affect the token budgets and representations underlying the reported results.
